title: The self that is never killed
hookLine: a warrior asks his charioteer to teach him, and the first lesson is about what in us can never die.
carry: the atman is never born and never dies

cards: A chariot stands alone in the open ground, with an army on either side, waiting. The warrior in it is a great archer, and he has just put his bow down.
The man holding the reins is his cousin and his friend, who agreed to come to this war without picking up a single weapon. Back in the Udyoga days, Arjuna chose Krishna that way, unarmed.
Now the choice pays off in a way no one planned. Session three of six: the moment a soldier becomes a student.

teach.h: STAND UP: A SOLDIER'S WORDS FAIL
teach.b: At the start of the Gita's second chapter, Krishna first tries a soldier's language. Shake off this weakness. Stand up.
It doesn't work. Arjuna answers with questions. How can he shoot arrows at Bhishma and Drona, men he should honor?
Better to live as a beggar.

teach.h: I AM YOUR DISCIPLE. TEACH ME.
teach.b: Then he says the line that changes everything: I am your disciple. Teach me. I've come to you for refuge.
He says he will not fight, and falls silent. And Krishna, as if smiling, there between the two armies, begins. You grieve for those you shouldn't grieve for.
There was never a time when I was not, nor you, nor these kings, and there will never be a time when we cease to be. The self in each of them is never born and never dies. Weapons can't cut it.
The body is set aside the way a person puts away worn clothes and takes up new ones.
This is one of Hinduism's biggest teachings: the atman, the true self, eternal, behind every face. It's why Hindus speak of rebirth, the self taking up a new body the way you take up new clothes.
And it's why, when someone dies, many Hindu families read from the Gita, often these very verses, at the bedside or at the prayer gathering. Read in place, it isn't a seminar on the soul.
It's an answer to one grieving man about real people across the field: his grandfather, his teacher, his kin.

how: The Gita's second chapter, with its verses on the self that is never born and never dies, is often read or recited when someone dies, at the bedside or at the prayer gathering afterward.

o: the second chapter of the Gita, where Arjuna turns student
the pledge Krishna made to drive the chariot but never fight
the book of the war, named for Bhishma, where the Gita is spoken

games.q: what was said in the chariot? tap the pairs.
p: I am your disciple. teach me.
you grieve for those you shouldn't
no weapon cuts it, no fire burns it

s: Arjuna agreed to fight as soon as Krishna told him to stand
he answered with questions, asked to be taught, and said he would not fight.
in the second chapter he says: I am your disciple, teach me.
Krishna taught that the self dies with the body
he taught the atman is never born and never dies; the body is set aside like worn clothes.

games.q: you're Arjuna. your driver tells you to shake off weakness and stand up. you still can't see how to fight your teachers. what do you do?
o: obey and pick up the bow.
ask him to be your teacher, and say you won't fight.
order him to drive you home.
games.why: Arjuna calls himself Krishna's disciple, asks to be taught, says he will not fight, and falls silent. then Krishna, as if smiling, begins.

practice: Many Hindus recite or listen to these verses for someone they've lost. Bring to mind someone you love who has died, or someone you're afraid of losing. Breathing in, picture their face.
Breathing out, hold Krishna's words gently: what was truly them was never born and never dies. If you pray, you can place them in God's keeping. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with love.

wordCard.voice: Bhishma Parva. The book of the battle where, before a single arrow flies, a soldier asks to be taught, and hears that the self can never be killed.
